h1: The 6 Best Glass Electric Kettles of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Glass Electric Kettles 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six glass electric kettles from 1.2L to 1.8L, including temperature-control and gooseneck models, with specs compared.
summary: The Amazon Basics glass carafe is the best value: 1.7 liters and 1500W for under $25. Tea and pour-over drinkers should step up to the Chefman with temperature control and a gooseneck spout. The Cuisinart offers variable temperature from a bigger brand, the 1.8 liter Chefman holds the most for little money, and the 1.2 liter Chefman suits desks and small kitchens.
intro: There is something oddly satisfying about watching water roll to a boil through glass, and that is exactly why people buy these kettles. The trouble is that the glass is only the body. The base, lid hinge, spout and controls decide how the kettle feels to use every day, and they vary far more between models than the carafe does.

So we looked past the glass. We reviewed six glass electric kettles, from basic 1.7 liter boilers to gooseneck models with temperature control, and scored each on the Primea framework. Capacity, wattage, temperature control and spout design carried the most weight, along with how much function each price bracket buys. The result is a clear split between plain boilers and kettles built for tea and coffee.

products.name: Amazon Basics Electric Kettle with Glass Carafe for Tea and Coffee
products.verdict: A 1.7 liter, 1500W glass kettle at under $25.
products.description:
The Amazon Basics glass carafe is the kettle we would buy for a kitchen that mostly boils water. It holds 1.7 liters, runs at 1500W and sells for under $25, which makes it the best price per liter of any kettle here.

It ranks first because it nails the basics at a price nobody else matches. It does not offer temperature control or a gooseneck, so it trails the Chefman for specialty tea and coffee. Against the 1.8 liter Chefman, it holds a little less, but both are plain boilers, and Amazon Basics edges ahead on overall balance.

Buy it if you want fast boiling water for mugs, noodles and French press coffee. The caveat is that glass shows limescale quickly, so plan on regular descaling in hard water areas.

products.name: Chefman Electric Kettle with Temperature Control
products.verdict: A 1.8 liter glass kettle with temperature control and a gooseneck spout.
products.description:
This Chefman is the glass kettle for people who care what temperature their water reaches. It holds 1.8 liters, offers temperature control and pours through a gooseneck spout. It sits in the $25 to $50 bracket.

It ranks second because it adds the two features that most improve tea and pour-over coffee, at a modest step up in price. The Amazon Basics is better value for plain boiling, and the Cuisinart below has a more established reputation, but the Chefman combines precision and capacity for less money than the Cuisinart.

Buy it if you brew green, white or oolong tea, or pour-over coffee. The caveat: the listing does not give a wattage figure, so we cannot tell you how quickly it boils compared with the 1500W picks.

products.name: Cuisinart 1.7L Glass Variable Temperature Control Electric Kettle
products.verdict: A 1.7 liter glass kettle with variable temperature control.
products.description:
Cuisinart's 1.7 liter glass kettle is built around variable temperature control, letting you set the water to suit delicate teas or coffee. It sits in the $50 to $100 bracket, the most expensive here.

It ranks third because the Chefman above offers temperature control plus a gooseneck for less money. What the Cuisinart brings is brand confidence and wide support from a long-running kitchen appliance maker. For some buyers that is worth the premium. The listing is light on other specs, which cost it a point on usability.

Buy it if you want temperature control from a familiar brand and do not need a gooseneck spout. Skip it if price matters, because the Chefman covers the same use for less. Check the base and lid materials on the listing before buying.

products.name: Chefman Electric Kettle
products.verdict: The largest glass kettle here at under $25.
products.description:
This Chefman is the biggest kettle in the ranking at 1.8 liters, with a 1500W element, all for under $25. It is a plain boiler with no temperature control.

It ranks fourth because it is functionally very close to the Amazon Basics at the top. It holds a touch more water, but neither offers anything beyond boiling, and the Amazon Basics scores slightly higher on overall balance. Against its sibling at number two, it gives up temperature control and the gooseneck to save money.

Buy it if your household boils a lot of water at once, for pasta, tea pots or several mugs in a row. Skip it if you brew delicate tea, because boiling water scorches green leaves. Like any glass carafe, it needs regular descaling in hard water areas.

products.name: GreenLife 1.7 Liter Electric Glass Kettle
products.verdict: A plain 1.7 liter glass kettle in the $25-50 bracket.
products.description:
GreenLife's glass kettle holds 1.7 liters and sits in the $25 to $50 bracket. The listing is plain and does not highlight temperature control, a gooseneck or a wattage figure.

It ranks fifth because the Amazon Basics matches its capacity for less, and the Chefman offers temperature control and a gooseneck in the same bracket. The GreenLife has to compete on design and brand loyalty, which matters to some buyers but is hard to score when features are missing.

Buy it if you already own GreenLife cookware and want a matching kettle. Skip it if you want the most kettle for your money, because both the Amazon Basics and the Chefman with temperature control are better buys on paper.

products.name: CHEFMAN Electric Kettle - 1.2L 1500W Hot Water Tea Pot with Infuser
products.verdict: A 1.2 liter, 1500W kettle with infuser and gooseneck spout.
products.description:
This compact Chefman holds 1.2 liters, runs at 1500W and pairs a gooseneck spout with a removable tea infuser. It sells for under $25.

It ranks last because of capacity. At 1.2 liters it serves one or two people well, but it is the smallest kettle in the group by a clear margin. Against the larger Chefman, it gains the infuser and a gooseneck but gives up capacity and temperature control.

Buy it for a desk, a dorm or a small kitchen where loose-leaf tea is the main use. The infuser and gooseneck make it a neat tea brewer for little money. Skip it if you regularly boil for three or more people.

whatMatters.detail: Capacity is how much water the kettle boils in one go. 1.7 liters covers six to seven mugs and suits most households, while 1.2 liters is better for one or two people. Check the liters figure in the title, and look at the max fill line in the photos, since usable volume can be a little less than the headline.

Different teas want different water temperatures. Green and white teas taste bitter if brewed with boiling water, while black tea and French press coffee need a full boil. Temperature control lets you stop the kettle below boiling. Look for temperature control or variable temperature in the title, as on the Chefman and Cuisinart models.

A gooseneck spout narrows the stream for slow, precise pouring over coffee grounds or loose tea. A standard spout pours faster and suits mugs and pots. If you brew pour-over, gooseneck is close to essential. Check the photos, since gooseneck is not always in the title. The Chefman at number two and the compact Chefman both have one.

Wattage sets how fast the kettle heats. On a standard US outlet, 1500W is common and quick, while lower ratings take longer. Look for the figure in the spec table. Several kettles here, including the Cuisinart and the temperature control Chefman, do not list wattage, so compare them on features rather than assuming speed.

Glass lets you see the water level and the boil, but the carafe gets hot and shows mineral scale clearly. The base, lid and handle are usually plastic or metal. Check the listing for what touches the water, especially the lid and filter. If you have hard water, expect to descale glass kettles more often than steel ones.

faq.a: Glass kettles are built from heat-resistant glass designed for repeated boiling. Avoid putting a hot carafe on a cold, wet surface, and check the listing for the glass type and care instructions. The Amazon Basics and Chefman listings both state the glass body clearly.

Yes, clearly. Glass shows every white ring of mineral build-up, especially in hard water areas. That is a feature if you want to know when to descale, and a drawback if you want the kettle to look spotless. Plan on regular cleaning with any of these.

Fill halfway with equal parts white vinegar and water, boil, then let it sit for 20 minutes. Rinse well and boil fresh water once or twice before use. Glass carafes like the Amazon Basics show you exactly when the scale is gone.

All kettles hiss and rumble as they approach a boil, and glass does not muffle that. In general noise is similar across these models. If you want quieter mornings, temperature control on the Chefman or Cuisinart lets you stop short of a full rolling boil.

Only if you brew delicate tea or care about pour-over coffee. For mugs and instant drinks, the Amazon Basics at a full boil is all you need. For green or white tea, the Chefman with temperature control is worth the extra money.

Most modern kettles switch off when the water boils or the carafe is lifted, but listings do not always say so clearly. Check the feature bullets on each listing before buying, especially if anyone in the house tends to forget the kettle.

finalTake: For plain boiling, the Amazon Basics glass carafe is the best buy: 1.7 liters and 1500W for very little money. Tea and pour-over drinkers should spend a bit more on the Chefman with temperature control and a gooseneck. The Cuisinart is the brand-name alternative, the 1.8 liter Chefman suits big households, and the compact Chefman with infuser is a smart desk kettle.
